children: By Emily Ou Yong
Iron ore futures traded in a narrow range on Tuesday, as a sharp drop in global shipments and arrivals at Chinese ports offset pressure from high inventories and weak steel-mill demand.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
was little changed at 684 yuan ($102.55) a metric ton.
The benchmark December iron ore (SZZFZ6) on the Singapore Exchange was 0.28% lower at $92.5 a ton.

Global iron ore shipments fell by 5.57 million tons from the previous week to 29.91 million tons in the week ended November 8, consultancy Mysteel data showed. Shipments from Australia and Brazil declined by 3.84 million tons to 24.06 million tons.
Arrivals at 47 Chinese ports dropped by 2.5 million tons over the same period to 27.64 million tons, according to Mysteel.
China's iron ore imports in October slid 3.8% from the month before, to a five-month low, data from the country's General Administration of Customs showed.

Declining shipments from short-term weather disruptions in Australia and Brazil have supported prices, but their impact is likely to be temporary and insufficient to alter the broader trend of ample supply, analysts at Galaxy Futures said in a note.
Iron ore inventories at major Chinese ports rose 0.52% week-on-week to 154.52 million tons on Friday, data from consultancy Steelhome showed.
Expectations of winter stockpiling are unlikely to offset elevated inventories, limiting the upside for iron ore prices, the Galaxy analysts said.

Hot-metal output continued to decline, while steel mills were replenishing stocks mainly to meet immediate needs, leaving little scope for demand growth, analysts at Shanghai Metals Market said in a note.
Other steelmaking ingredients on the DCE traded sideways, with coking coal
NYMEX:ACT1!
little changed and coke (DCJcv1) up 0.1%.
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange were little changed. Rebar
fell 0.1%, hot-rolled coil
edged 0.16% lower and stainless steel
was flat.
($1 = 6.6702 Chinese yuan)
